claims.text: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered single-phase BCC solid solution.
Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo has a room-temperature compressive yield strength of approximately 1719 MPa.
Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo has a room-temperature compressive ductile strain of approximately 5–10%.
The limited plasticity of equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is caused by its high Mo content and the associated increase in electronegativity difference.
Replacing approximately 50% of the Mo with V produces NbZrTiHfMo0.5V0.5.
Replacing approximately 50% of Mo with V will reduce the alloy's overall electronegativity difference.
NbZrTiHfMo0.5V0.5 can retain a homogeneous, single-phase disordered BCC structure after homogenization and quenching.
A reduced electronegativity difference will lower electric-charge disparity and lattice friction.
Lower electric-charge disparity and lattice friction will reduce atomistic barriers to dislocation motion and enhance dislocation mobility.
The modified alloy will retain strong solid-solution strengthening despite its reduced Mo content.
NbZrTiHfMo0.5V0.5 will exhibit a room-temperature compressive ductile strain of approximately 15–20%.
NbZrTiHfMo0.5V0.5 will maintain a room-temperature compressive yield strength near 1700 MPa.
The beneficial strength–plasticity effect depends on retaining a single-phase disordered BCC structure and avoiding deleterious phase transformations.
Unexpected precipitation or phase separation could reduce both strength and plasticity.
The proposed alloy should be vacuum arc melted, homogenized at approximately 1200–1300 °C for several hours, and water quenched.
XRD, SEM, and TEM can be used to test for a homogeneous single-phase BCC microstructure and unwanted precipitates.
Room-temperature compression testing can measure whether the modified alloy reaches the predicted yield strength and ductile strain.
